points: Add a designer (Opus, writes HTML mockups, write scope limited to design mockups) and a design-reviewer (Opus, since cost is no limit and visual judgment is where the strongest model pays off; it opens every screenshot). Skip a ux-builder: building to a mockup is ordinary builder work.
Route with one test: does this lane touch a screen? If yes, the designer runs before the build and design-review after it. Nothing else changes.
Keep builders, reviewers and test authors separate. A builder can't fairly review itself, and builders-cannot-edit-tests stops weakened tests. Solo mode is the right valve for small changes.

Haiku at xhigh is fine for round-1 code review, where tests and CI catch what it misses. Not for screens: nothing downstream checks taste. To prove it, rerun a few past design-review screenshots through Haiku and Sonnet and compare.

Don't add more agent kinds now; process load is the problem. Collections like wshobson/agents and VoltAgent are reading material for prompts, not installs. The roundup found no design reviewer agents in them.
An agent that improves agents tends to add rules. Make it a pruner, and change an agent only when an eval shows the new version is better (skill-creator benchmarks, claude plugin eval).

Token cost: frontend-design is about 1,500 words and impeccable's polish, layout and animate references about 2,500. Screenshots cost more (pages x sizes x themes x reviewers), so run design-review only on screen diffs, at the sizes each repo ships.
With cost no limit, the Sonnet ceiling still makes sense for speed on routine work. Spend Opus where judgment is the point: planning, designing, and judging screens.
summary: Which agents to add, which not, and why.
title: Roles and agents
